questions.enonce_markdown: A train travels along a straight horizontal road between two stations $A$ and $B$ which are $6300\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. The train starts from rest at $A$ and moves with constant acceleration $0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ until it reaches a speed $v\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, ($v < 50$). The train then maintains this speed for a time $t$ and then decelerates uniformly at $0.25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and comes to rest at $B$. The total time for the journey is $300\ \mathrm{s}$. Find $t$ in terms of $v$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model.** The motion is in three stages along the straight track (positive direction from $A$ to $B$): acceleration at $0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ from rest to $v$, constant speed $v$ for $t$ seconds, deceleration at $0.25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ from $v$ to rest. Use $v = u + at$ in stages 1 and 3.

**Stage 1:** $v = 0 + 0.5\,t_1 \Rightarrow t_1 = 2v$.

**Stage 3:** $0 = v - 0.25\,t_3 \Rightarrow t_3 = 4v$.

**Total time:**

$$t_1 + t + t_3 = 300 \;\Rightarrow\; 2v + t + 4v = 300$$

**$t = 300 - 6v$ (seconds).**

questions.enonce_markdown: A train travels along a straight horizontal road between two stations $A$ and $B$ which are $6300\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. The train starts from rest at $A$ and moves with constant acceleration $0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ until it reaches a speed $v\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, ($v < 50$). The train then maintains this speed for a time $t$ and then decelerates uniformly at $0.25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and comes to rest at $B$. The total time for the journey is $300\ \mathrm{s}$. Calculate the value of $v$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Distances in the three stages** (using $s = \dfrac{v^{2} - u^{2}}{2a}$ for stages 1 and 3 and $s = vt$ for stage 2, with $t = 300 - 6v$ from part (a)):

$$s_1 = \frac{v^{2}}{2(0.5)} = v^{2},\qquad s_2 = v\,t = v(300 - 6v),\qquad s_3 = \frac{v^{2}}{2(0.25)} = 2v^{2}$$

**Total distance $= 6300\ \mathrm{m}$:**

$$v^{2} + 300v - 6v^{2} + 2v^{2} = 6300 \;\Rightarrow\; -3v^{2} + 300v - 6300 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; v^{2} - 100v + 2100 = 0$$

$$(v - 30)(v - 70) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; v = 30\ \text{or}\ v = 70$$

The question states $v < 50$, so $v = 70$ is rejected (it would also give $t = 300 - 420 < 0$).

**Check** with $v = 30$: $t = 300 - 180 = 120\ \mathrm{s}$; $s_1 = 900\ \mathrm{m}$, $s_2 = 30\times 120 = 3600\ \mathrm{m}$, $s_3 = 1800\ \mathrm{m}$; total $= 6300\ \mathrm{m}$ as required. (The same equation comes from the area of the speed-time trapezium, $\tfrac12(300 + t)\,v = 6300$.)

**$v = 30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (and $t = 120\ \mathrm{s}$).**

questions.enonce_markdown: A uniform ladder $AB$ of length $5\ \mathrm{m}$ and weight $200\ \mathrm{N}$ rests with the end $B$ on a smooth vertical wall and the other end $A$ on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of friction between the ladder and the floor is $\tfrac{1}{3}$. The ladder makes an angle $\alpha$ with the wall, where $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{5}{12}\right)$. Find how far a man of weight $600\ \mathrm{N}$ will go up the ladder before it starts to slip.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Diagram (described).** The ladder $AB$ leans against the vertical wall, $A$ on the floor, $B$ on the wall, making angle $\alpha$ with the wall (the vertical), where $\tan\alpha = \tfrac{5}{12}$, so $\sin\alpha = \tfrac{5}{13}$ and $\cos\alpha = \tfrac{12}{13}$. Forces: at $A$, the normal reaction $R$ upwards and the friction $F$ horizontally towards the wall (friction opposes the tendency of $A$ to slide away from the wall); at $B$, the reaction $S$ of the smooth wall, horizontal and away from the wall; the weight $200\ \mathrm{N}$ of the ladder acting at its midpoint $G$, $2.5\ \mathrm{m}$ from $A$; the weight $600\ \mathrm{N}$ of the man acting at a distance $x$ metres from $A$ along the ladder.

**Resolve vertically:** $R = 200 + 600 = 800\ \mathrm{N}$.

**Resolve horizontally:** $F = S$.

**Limiting friction (about to slip):** $F = \mu R = \tfrac13\times 800 = \tfrac{800}{3}\ \mathrm{N}$, so $S = \tfrac{800}{3}\ \mathrm{N}$.

**Moments about $A$** (a point at distance $d$ along the ladder has horizontal distance $d\sin\alpha$ from $A$, and $B$ is at height $5\cos\alpha$ above the floor):

$$S\,(5\cos\alpha) = 200\,(2.5\sin\alpha) + 600\,(x\sin\alpha)$$

Substituting $\cos\alpha = \tfrac{12}{13}$, $\sin\alpha = \tfrac{5}{13}$:

$$\frac{800}{3}\times\frac{60}{13} = (500 + 600x)\times\frac{5}{13} \;\Rightarrow\; 16\,000 = 5(500 + 600x)$$

$$3200 = 500 + 600x \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{2700}{600} = 4.5$$

For a larger $x$ the moment needed at $B$, and hence the friction required, would exceed the limiting value, so the ladder would slip. Since $4.5 < 5$, the man can indeed be on the ladder at this point.

**The man can go $4.5\ \mathrm{m}$ up the ladder (measured from $A$ along the ladder) before it starts to slip.**
